name: Precision bias
statement: A number stated precisely is treated as better founded than a round one, so precise offers and anchors move other people's numbers further.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and only one of them has been measured. The broad claim is that precision implies accuracy, so a figure given to the decimal place is nearer the truth than a rounded one. No study of a construct by the name 'precision bias' was located in these searches. The narrow claim does have a literature, under the names anchor precision and the price precision effect. It says that a number expressed precisely exerts more pull on somebody else's number than a round number of the same size. Janiszewski and Uy put the mechanism in the arithmetic. Their abstract argues that a precise anchor is represented on a subjective scale with a finer resolution, so each mental step away from it is smaller and the total correction is smaller. Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames put it in the social inference instead. A negotiator who opens at $4,885 seems to have worked something out, and one who opens at $5,000 seems to have guessed. The two accounts agree on the direction and disagree about who the effect should fail for.

origin.note: No publication coining the phrase 'precision bias' was located. Janiszewski and Uy's five studies are the root of the effect the phrase is applied to, and their paper does not use the phrase in its title or abstract. Wikipedia's article opens by calling precision bias a cognitive bias and cites for that a page range in the proceedings of the 2011 Cognitive Science Society meeting, given with no title and no authors.

evidence:
Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames ran six studies on first offers. Studies 1a to 1d were vignettes: recipients of a round offer adjusted further in their counteroffer than recipients of a precise offer of similar size. Adjustments were $9.53 against $7.94 and $8.39 on a $20 jewellery offer, $2.56 against $1.77 and $2.19 on a $10 coffee contract, $4.36 against $3.15 and $3.85 on a $10 restaurant contract, and $10.56 against $7.19 and $8.08 on a $20 textbook. Partial eta squared ran from .030 to .073 across the four. Study 2 put 130 buyer-seller dyads of managers, MBAs and undergraduates through a live car negotiation. Sellers facing a precise opening offer countered $3,197 away from it against $4,235 for round openings, t(69) = 2.39, p = .020, d = .57. The gap survived to the settlement, at $2,256 against $2,963, t(69) = 2.043, p = .045, d = .49. Study 3 gave 238 MTurk sellers a $2,000, $1,865 or $2,135 offer for a used car and measured whether the buyer seemed to have researched the price. Precision raised that rating, the rating predicted smaller adjustments, and the indirect effect had a 95% bias-corrected bootstrap interval of 3.49 to 40.68.

The authors also counted how offers are actually phrased. Of 356 opening offers made by 113 executives and 243 MBA students in class exercises, 48% carried a single significant digit, 49% carried two, and none was specified to the dollar. Of 1,511 Zillow listings in four American cities, 73% of homes between $10,000 and $99,999 ended in at least three zeros, as did 98% of homes between $1m and $10m.

The effect has been found on prices as well as offers. Thomas, Simon and Kadiyali report five studies in which buyers underestimate the magnitude of precise prices. Their participants judged $395,425 to be smaller than $395,000; a nationally representative sample of homeowners was willing to pay more for houses priced at $364,578 than at $365,000; and buyers in two residential property markets paid higher sale prices where list prices were more precise. Those figures come from the paper's abstract, which was the only part obtained.

Hukkanen and Keloharju looked at 1,769 initial all-cash takeover bids for listed American targets announced between 1985 and 2012. About 14% were priced to the nearest five dollars a share and about half to the nearest dollar, with only a sixth finer than a quarter. Bids at five-dollar precision moved 17.6% on average from opening to final price, against 6.0% for bids finer than a quarter. A bid finer than a quarter was 8% more likely to close than a five-dollar bid and 6% more likely than a one-dollar bid. On the median transaction the round pricing is worth $4m to $5m more paid for the target.

replication.headline: A preregistered study of 400 estate agents reproduced the negotiation effect, and three experiments with 1,505 Danes found no precision effect on trust in official numbers.
replication.detail:
Frech, Loschelder and Friese preregistered a field experiment with 400 professional real-estate agents, who negotiated over a house inside their expertise or a motor yacht outside it. Their abstract reports that they replicated the advantageous anchor precision effect, that too much precision backfired in both domains, and that the effect ran through competence attributed to the opponent. It is a replication of Loschelder, Friese, Schaerer and Galinsky, whose five experiments covered 1,320 experts and amateurs in real-estate, jewellery, car and human-resources negotiations. That paper's abstract reports positive linear effects of precision for amateurs and inverted-U effects for experts, with the downturn removed when the first mover justified the number. Both are quoted here from their abstracts at PubMed.

Schultze and Loschelder moved the question to advice taking, preregistered, with 195 students estimating the lengths of 30 rivers. Advisers gave moderate, high or extreme precision, and the advice taking score rose from 0.34 to 0.41 to 0.42, F(2, 388) = 27.26, p < .001, eta squared = .03. Extreme precision did not backfire, even when the advice read 3,461.73 km. The authors treat the pattern as a monotone increase that flattens rather than an inverted U.

Olsen found nothing in a political setting. Three experiments were embedded in one YouGov survey of 1,505 Danes. Asked which of two economic forecasts they trusted, 76.4% preferred a round 1.5% growth rate to a precise 1.537%, and 57.7% preferred a round 20bn kroner deficit to a precise 20.37bn. Asked to rate confidence in single numbers, they gave 4.7 to both the precise and the round budget figure, 3.8 to both unemployment figures, and more to the round growth rate than the precise one, 5.2 against 4.8, t(754) = 2.5, p = .013. Of the three long-term policy goals in the third experiment, only public expenditure showed a precision effect, F(1, 1501) = 8.42, p < .01, and Olsen notes that the accompanying frame manipulation moved nothing, which he treats as a reason for caution. His summary is that no clear evidence of a precision effect appeared in politics.

study.cite: Frech, M.-L., Loschelder, D. D., & Friese, M. (2019). How and why different forms of expertise moderate anchor precision in price decisions: A pre-registered field experiment. Experimental Psychology, 66(2), 165-175.

limits:
The largest meta-analysis of anchoring declined to test this moderator. Roseler and Schutz pooled 393 effect sizes from 17,708 participants and report anchoring at g = 0.689, 95% CI 0.589 to 0.789. They coded anchor precision by whether the last digit was zero, found that anchors close to the true value were being coded precise more often, and write that they therefore chose not to analyse precision. So the pooled evidence on anchoring says nothing either way about this claim, and the entry rests on individual studies.

The effect is not uniform in size or sign. Loschelder and colleagues report it reversing above a point for experts, Olsen reports its absence across three political experiments, and Schultze and Loschelder report a small one, eta squared of .03, that stops rising rather than reversing. Mason and colleagues' own vignette studies used MTurk samples of 238 to 280 answering hypothetical questions about jewellery, coffee and textbooks.

Hukkanen and Keloharju's takeover results are associations in observational data and the authors present them as such. Their figures here are read from Harvard Business School working paper 16-058, dated 2 November 2015; the article was published in Financial Management in 2019 and that version was not obtained, so the numbers may have moved.

Several papers could not be read. Janiszewski and Uy, Loschelder and colleagues, Frech and colleagues, and Thomas, Simon and Kadiyali are all paywalled, and this entry uses their abstracts at PubMed or Crossref. Jerez-Fernandez, Angulo and Oppenheimer, the paper Wikipedia leans on hardest, carries no abstract at PubMed and its full text was not obtained, so nothing from it is reported here as a finding. Searches for the term itself covered Crossref title and bibliographic queries, PubMed and web search; OpenAlex was tried and returned a rate-limit error. Crossref and PubMed hits on the exact phrase are about measurement error in chemistry, radiocarbon dating, textiles and clinical assays.
misreadings:
The name is the first thing to get wrong. Precision bias is a term of bias catalogues rather than of research psychology, and the studies behind it were published under other names: anchor precision, the price precision effect, the too-much-precision effect. An entry that treats it as a single measured construct is describing a heading rather than a finding, in the way the affinity-bias entry here describes one.

Wikipedia's article, the main source of the popular version, contains three attributions its cited papers do not support. It credits Janiszewski and Uy with an analysis of 12,581 Florida home sales; their abstract describes five studies of adjustment away from anchors, and the analysis of residential property transactions belongs to Thomas, Simon and Kadiyali's Study 5. It says Mason and colleagues found precise offers reduced the likelihood of a counteroffer being made at all; that paper, read in full here, measures the size of counteroffers and the final settlement price and reports no such measure. It cites Peters, Markowitz, Nadratowski and Shoots-Reinhard on climate posts as evidence about precision. That study contrasts posts containing an Arabic integer with posts using verbal terms such as 'almost all'. The comparison is between numbers and words, not between precise and round numbers.

The effect is a moderator of anchoring, not a rival to it. Anchoring says the number pulls; precision says a finer-grained number pulls harder. Both entries are here, and the anchoring evidence is far stronger than the precision evidence.

It is also not the 99-ending price. Charm pricing turns on the leading digit changing between $3.99 and $4.00, and it has its own entry here with its own meta-analysis. The precision claim concerns numbers of the same leading digits differing in how many of the trailing ones are zero, such as $364,578 against $365,000.

The practical advice usually drawn from it runs past the evidence. Mason and colleagues say plainly that they did not test the risks, and list two: that an overly precise offer might signal inflexibility and cause avoidable impasses, and that it could be read as a manipulative gambit. Loschelder and colleagues then found the second of those happening with experts. Olsen found that a Danish electorate trusted the round growth forecast more than the precise one.

Mason, M. F., Lee, A. J., Wiley, E. A., & Ames, D. R. (2013). Precise offers are potent anchors: Conciliatory counteroffers and attributions of knowledge in negotiations. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 49(4), 759-763. Read in full from the accepted manuscript hosted on Ames's Columbia page.

Loschelder, D. D., Friese, M., Schaerer, M., & Galinsky, A. D. (2016). The too-much-precision effect: When and why precise anchors backfire with experts. Psychological Science, 27(12), 1573-1587. Paywalled; described here from its abstract at PubMed.

Frech, M.-L., Loschelder, D. D., & Friese, M. (2019). How and why different forms of expertise moderate anchor precision in price decisions: A pre-registered field experiment. Experimental Psychology, 66(2), 165-175. Paywalled and blocked at the publisher; described here from its abstract at PubMed.

Schultze, T., & Loschelder, D. D. (2021). How numeric advice precision affects advice taking. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 34(3), 303-310. Read in full from the open-access version of record at Queen's University Belfast.

Olsen, A. L. (2018). Precise performance: Do citizens rely on numerical precision as a cue of confidence? Journal of Behavioral Public Administration, 1(1), 1-10. Read in full; the source of the three null experiments.

Roseler, L., & Schutz, A. (2022). Hanging the anchor off a new ship: A meta-analysis of anchoring effects. PsyArXiv preprint, 9 March 2022. Read in full; the source of the pooled anchoring estimate and of the decision not to code anchor precision.

Thomas, M., Simon, D. H., & Kadiyali, V. (2010). The price precision effect: Evidence from laboratory and market data. Marketing Science, 29(1), 175-190. Paywalled; described here from the abstract carried by Crossref.

Hukkanen, P., & Keloharju, M. (2019). Initial offer precision and M&A outcomes. Financial Management, 48(1), 291-310. The published version was not obtained; the figures here are read from Harvard Business School working paper 16-058, dated 2 November 2015.

Peters, E., Markowitz, D. M., Nadratowski, A., & Shoots-Reinhard, B. (2024). Numeric social-media posts engage people with climate science. PNAS Nexus, 3(7). Cited only because Wikipedia offers it as evidence about precision; described from its abstract at Crossref, which contrasts Arabic integers with verbal terms.

Jerez-Fernandez, A., Angulo, A. N., & Oppenheimer, D. M. (2014). Show me the numbers: Precision as a cue to others' confidence. Psychological Science, 25(2), 633-635. The paper Wikipedia cites most; paywalled, no abstract at PubMed, and not read, so no finding from it appears on this page.
Wikipedia, 'Precision bias'. Checked for a coinage claim and as the source of the popular version. Its wikitext was read on 10 August 2026. An index, not a source for any finding on this page.
